findings.message: Option c is self-defeating on its face: it claims the 5-minute TTL is expiring *because* turns finish faster, which a learner can eliminate without any knowledge of caching (shorter turns mean less elapsed time, not more). No plausible learner would select it.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a plausible TTL-based distractor, e.g. "The cache entry uses the 5-minute TTL and the harness's batching means some turns arrive more than 5 minutes after the last write."

findings.message: The explanation names "Fable 5.1" alongside "Opus 5" as a model supporting a per-message effort system message; "Fable" is not an Anthropic Claude model family, so this claim cannot be verified by a learner and risks teaching a non-existent model name.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the unverifiable model name and state the capability generically, e.g. "...or, on models that expose per-message effort control, set effort per message so the cached prefix is preserved."

findings.message: Option C's text is word-for-word identical to keyed option A (plus "Record the change in the team's runbook"), so it performs the same documented fix and is equally correct; a learner cannot pick a single answer. Option C's "why" (about changing model behaviour and cost, and thinking always being on) clearly belongs to a "disable extended thinking" option, confirming the option text was swapped in by mistake.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore option C's intended text, e.g. "Disable extended thinking for the agent so no thinking or redacted_thinking blocks are produced.", which matches its existing "why" and leaves A as the only correct, least-change fix.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks how Messages API streaming works (SSE vs WebSockets) and when the SDK requires streaming, but the answer text describes the difference between client tools and server tools. A learner is given no correct answer to the question asked, and the code snippet and realWorldUsage note (SSE proxying) both contradict the explanation's subject.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with content matching the stem, e.g.: "The Messages API has no WebSocket endpoint. Streaming is plain HTTP Server-Sent Events: set stream=true (or use client.messages.stream in the SDK) and read the event sequence message_start, content_block_start, content_block_delta, content_block_stop, message_delta, message_stop, plus periodic ping and possible error events. The SDK requires streaming for long-running requests — a non-streaming request whose estimated generation time exceeds the 10-minute limit (large max_tokens on slower models) is rejected, so the SDK raises an error telling you to stream and use stream.get_final_message() to reassemble the response."

findings.message: The keying is inverted: option c ("wait for requests to start failing after retirement") is marked correct even though it is plainly wrong and its own "why" text argues against it, while option a (Console usage export by API key and model plus the 60-day notice) is marked incorrect despite being the approach the explanation endorses.
findings.suggestedFix: Set option a "correct": true and give it a supporting rationale, and set option c "correct": false, keeping its existing "why" as the distractor rationale.

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is copied verbatim from the first sentence of the explanation and hands the learner one of the four required mappings (CSV → built-in code execution server tool) before they answer, so part of the question answers itself.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the hint, or replace it with a non-answering cue such as "Hint: consider for each request whether Anthropic already hosts the capability, whether the logic is private to one app, whether it is procedural knowledge, and whether an external system must be shared across apps."

findings.message: "Claude Fable 5.1" (claude-fable-5-1, $10/$50) is not a real Claude model; Anthropic's model family uses only the Haiku / Sonnet / Opus tiers, with Opus as the top-capability, highest-priced tier. Listing a non-existent tier priced above Opus also contradicts the card's own description of Opus 5 as the model for complex agentic and enterprise work, so a learner would memorize a fabricated model ID and price.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the "Claude Fable 5.1 / claude-fable-5-1" entry and describe only the real lineup (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku tiers) with their verified API IDs, prices, context windows and max output, citing the Anthropic models overview page as the source.

findings.message: The stem appends a hint that quotes the keyed option's opening words verbatim ("Mark the rulebook with a one-hour cache_control block, submit a ..."), so a learner with no knowledge of prompt caching can identify option c by string matching alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the entire "Hint: the correct option begins ..." line from the question stem.

findings.message: Option b's "why" gives a false rationale: max_tokens must be at least 1 in every Messages API request, so a value of 0 is invalid in the synchronous API too, and there is no max_tokens: 0 "pre-warm mechanism" that "belongs to the synchronous API".
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the why as: "max_tokens must be >= 1, so this request is rejected outright; more importantly, a single batch gives no ordering guarantee, so even a valid seed request inside the same batch would not reliably run first."

findings.message: Option D states exactly the same action as the keyed option A ("Move the contract to the top of the prompt inside <document> tags and put the question as the last line"), merely prefixed with "Adopt this approach:", so two options are equally correct and the learner cannot pick a single answer. Option D's "why" (about a larger window / 1M-token models) does not match its own text, indicating the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option D's text with the distractor its rationale describes, e.g. "Switch to a Claude model with a 1M-token context window and send the prompt unchanged."

findings.message: The stem appends a hint that quotes the opening words of the keyed option verbatim ("Create a CloudFormation StackSet with service-managed permissions from the management ..."), so a learner with no knowledge of the topic can select option A by text matching alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the entire "Hint: the correct option begins ..." sentence from the question stem.

findings.message: Option C (Elastic Beanstalk to create an environment per account containing the baseline) is implausible for deploying CloudTrail/Config/GuardDuty/IAM governance resources and would not be considered by any learner.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a plausible distractor, e.g. "Use AWS Control Tower Account Factory customizations only, without drift reporting on the baseline resources" or "Use self-managed StackSet permissions and add each new account's target manually."

findings.message: Option D repeats option A's text verbatim ("Point the reporting application at the cluster's reader endpoint and attach an Aurora Auto Scaling policy...") but is keyed false, so two options are equally correct and the learner cannot pick a single answer. Its "why" also describes RDS Proxy, which the option text never mentions.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option D with the RDS Proxy distractor its rationale assumes, e.g. "Put an Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the cluster and point the reporting application at the proxy endpoint."

findings.message: The explanation discusses distractors that do not appear in the option set (RDS Proxy, an RDS Multi-AZ standby, and it states "The distractor is the instance endpoint", though no instance-endpoint option exists), which will confuse learners reviewing the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim the explanation to address only the options actually presented (reader endpoint + Auto Scaling, cluster endpoint, vertical scaling of the writer, and whatever option replaces D).

findings.message: The distractor "why" texts are prefixed with internal authoring-taxonomy labels ("Brute-force model swap:", "Mechanism for the wrong scope:", "Real technical error variable:") that are meaningless to a learner; the last one in particular is not intelligible English in context.
findings.suggestedFix: Strip the taxonomy prefixes so each "why" begins with the explanation, e.g. option d: "Strict mode guarantees the shape of a tool's input once the tool is chosen, not the choice of tool; the wrong tool would simply be called with perfectly valid arguments."

findings.message: Option C's text is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option A (only prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), so two options state the same correct solution and no single answer can be chosen; C's "why" instead describes AWS Global Accelerator, which its text never mentions.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C's text with the Global Accelerator distractor its rationale describes, e.g. "Put an AWS Global Accelerator in front of the bucket and give viewers the accelerator's static IPs so traffic enters the AWS backbone at the nearest edge."

findings.message: The explanation credits Rekognition with detecting "printed and handwritten" text. Rekognition's DetectText/text-in-video is scene-text detection for short, printed text (signs, captions, license plates) and is explicitly not intended for handwriting or dense document text — handwriting extraction is an Amazon Textract capability, which is exactly the Rekognition-vs-Textract distinction this card is meant to teach.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "printed and handwritten text" to "short printed text in scenes and images (signs, captions, license plates)" and keep the contrast that handwriting and dense document text belong to Textract.

findings.message: The stem asks "what controls who can trigger one?" and the accompanying code snippet literally shows `disable-model-invocation: true`, so a learner with no knowledge of Skills can read the second half of the answer straight off the card.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the `disable-model-invocation: true` line from the snippet (leave name/description/allowed-tools/argument-hint) and let the explanation introduce it, or split the invocation-control question onto a separate card without that snippet.

findings.message: The snippet's `allowed-tools` value uses a non-documented syntax: Claude Code frontmatter expects a comma-separated list with colon-prefixed Bash prefix patterns, so `Bash(git tag *) Bash(gh release *)` is neither comma-separated nor a valid prefix pattern and would not grant the intended permissions.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: `allowed-tools: Bash(git tag:*), Bash(gh release:*)`

findings.message: The snippet is shown with no file path, yet the explanation's main structural point is that a skill must live at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md; as written the frontmatter could just as easily be read as a slash-command file, which undercuts the lesson.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a path comment as the first line of the snippet, e.g. `<!-- .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md -->`.

findings.message: The realWorldUsage line says canUseTool is "the callback that runs after it [the decision]", which mischaracterizes it: canUseTool is invoked as part of the permission decision for calls not already resolved by allow/deny rules or the permission mode, not after a decision has been made.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "Unconditional policy belongs in the PreToolUse hook, which runs before any permission rule is applied, not in canUseTool, which is only consulted for calls that allow rules and the permission mode have not already resolved."

findings.message: The answer states that a user-defined (custom) tool has three required fields including `description`. In the Messages API tool schema only `name` and `input_schema` are required; `description` is optional (strongly recommended, but omitting it does not cause a validation error).
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "A custom tool definition has two API-required fields — name (must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$) and input_schema (a JSON Schema object for the parameters) — plus description, which is optional in the schema but strongly recommended in practice...", and change the stem to ask for "the core fields of a user-defined tool" rather than "the three required fields".

findings.message: The card keys option B (duplicate stack in a second Region with Route 53 failover) as correct, but that is not the MOST cost-effective way to survive the loss of one Availability Zone — and the explanation, the stem (which attributes the second-Region idea to an engineer's proposal to be corrected), and option B's own "why" text all state that the correct change is option A (add subnets in additional AZs to the Auto Scaling group and enable those zones on the ALB). As keyed, the card teaches a false answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option A and "correct": false on option B, leave option B's existing "why" (which already explains why a second Region is wrong) in place, and set option A's "why" to null.

findings.message: The explanation states the Intelligent-Tiering monitoring fee as "$0.0025 per 1,000 objects" without the billing period; the charge is $0.0025 per 1,000 objects per month, and omitting "per month" could lead a learner to read it as a one-time fee.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "a monitoring and automation fee of $0.0025 per 1,000 objects per month".

findings.message: The stem's distinctive figure "120,000 sustained IOPS" is reproduced verbatim only in the keyed option ("provisioned with 120,000 IOPS"); no other option carries a number, so a learner with no EBS knowledge can pick the key by surface number-matching alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the number from the key (e.g. "A Provisioned IOPS SSD io2 Block Express volume provisioned for the required IOPS") or add comparable figures to the distractors (e.g. "A gp3 volume provisioned to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s", "An st1 volume sized at 16 TiB").

findings.message: Option b's rationale states gp3 "tops out at 16,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s per volume"; gp3's maximum throughput is 1,000 MiB/s per volume, so the card teaches an incorrect figure.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "gp3 tops out at 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s per volume and offers single-digit millisecond latency...".

findings.message: The explanation and option b's rationale assert a hard API behavior — "Temperature is rejected on 4.7 and later models" / "Non-default temperature returns a 400 on Sonnet 5" — which does not match documented Messages API behavior, where temperature accepts 0.0–1.0 and is only pinned to 1 when extended thinking is enabled. The distractor is already wrong on the substantive point (randomness reduces format consistency), so the questionable 400-error claim adds an unverifiable fact.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to the defensible point, e.g. explanation: "Raising temperature adds randomness and would make the layout less consistent (and with extended thinking enabled temperature must stay at 1)." Option b why: "Higher temperature increases variation, so layout drift would get worse, not better; it is not a format-control lever."

findings.message: The qualifier "MOST cost-effective" does not discriminate among the options: cost/token usage is essentially identical for all four invocations, and the simpler options (b `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, d `--permission-mode auto`) require no allowlist configuration and so are at least as cost-effective as the key. The real deciding criterion in the stem is enforced least privilege (execute nothing beyond `npm test` and file reads), not cost, so the keyed answer wins on a criterion the qualifier does not name.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier to match the actual discriminator, e.g. "Which invocation enforces the requirement with the LEAST privilege granted?" or "Which invocation meets the security team's requirement?" and update "qualifier" from "MOST cost-effective" to "LEAST privilege".

findings.message: The sentence about the size cap is garbled and unreadable ("256 KB for years, and the figure exam questions still use, and that is still the current quota"), which obscures the key fact that the 256 KB body limit is a current hard quota.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "Bodies have a hard cap of 256 KB, which is still the current quota and the figure exam questions use."

findings.message: The stem asks what you change, but the answer only says to "raise it when consumers lag" without giving the concrete setting needed for the stated one-week outage.
findings.suggestedFix: State the change explicitly: set MessageRetentionPeriod to at least 604800 seconds (7 days), up to the 14-day maximum.

findings.message: The keyed answer is option c (attach a second virtual private gateway), which is factually wrong — a VPC can have only one virtual private gateway attached, and a second AWS-side gateway does nothing for a failed on-premises device; option c's own "why" text and the explanation both say this. The correct design is option a (second customer gateway device plus a second Site-to-Site VPN connection to the same VGW with BGP), which is marked correct: false and has a null "why".
findings.suggestedFix: Invert the keying: set option a to "correct": true with "why": null, and set option c to "correct": false keeping its existing "why" text explaining that only one virtual private gateway can be attached to a VPC and that it does not address a customer-side device failure.

findings.message: Option (c)'s rationale is incoherent as an explanation of why the option is wrong: "the docs say to set the limits as well, because Claude Code enforces them however Claude decides to delegate" garbles the point and even reads as if Claude Code does enforce prompt instructions. The real reason is that prompt text is advisory and provides no hard, programmatic ceiling on cost or nesting depth.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the why as: "System-prompt wording is only a suggestion to the model — nothing enforces it. A run can still exceed the wording and spend unbounded dollars, so it gives no hard ceiling on cost or nesting depth."

findings.message: Option B repeats option A verbatim ("Set the automated backup retention period to 30 days and rely on point-in-time recovery.") and only adds a harmless runbook note, so it is equally correct while only A is keyed; a learner cannot pick a single answer. Its "why" also describes hourly manual snapshots, which its text never mentions, indicating the intended option text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore the intended distractor for option B, e.g. "Take hourly manual snapshots of the DB instance and retain them for 30 days.", which matches the existing "why" rationale.

findings.message: The explanation refutes a "Multi-AZ standby" choice, but no option offers Multi-AZ, so the explanation does not match the option set.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the clause "a Multi-AZ standby is availability, not backup" from the explanation (or add a Multi-AZ distractor option).

findings.message: The explanation calls Quick Sight "the business intelligence feature of Amazon Quick" — the umbrella product is named Amazon Quick Suite, not "Amazon Quick", so the service name given to learners is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "Use Amazon Quick Sight, the business intelligence capability of Amazon Quick Suite and the successor to Amazon QuickSight."

findings.message: Option F ("AWS Glue ETL jobs written to answer each ad hoc query") is implausible on its face — writing an ETL job per ad hoc question is obviously not an interactive SQL path, so no learner would select it, and it adds no discrimination to a question about Athena vs. Redshift vs. EMR.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option F with a plausible near-miss, e.g. "Amazon Redshift Spectrum alone, with no Glue Data Catalog, for the ad hoc team's S3 files" or "Amazon Athena for both the ad hoc queries and the nightly multi-table joins", and give a 'why' that explains the real trade-off.

findings.message: The explanation misspells the service name as "Amazon Quick Sight"; the product is "Amazon QuickSight" (one word).
findings.suggestedFix: Change "Amazon Quick Sight builds dashboards" to "Amazon QuickSight builds dashboards".

findings.message: Option c's text is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option b (Message Batches API, two batches of at most 100,000 requests keyed by custom_id), so two identical options exist with one marked correct and one marked incorrect — a learner cannot pick a single answer. Option c's "why" discusses prompt caching, indicating the intended caching option text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c's text with the intended caching distractor, e.g. "Keep the synchronous Messages API but enable prompt caching on the classification instructions so repeated prefix tokens are billed at the cache-read rate." (its existing "why" then matches).

findings.message: The keyed option's arithmetic is inconsistent with the stem: of the five listed steps, "validate the totals in code" is a programmatic check, so the chain is four LLM calls plus one code gate, not "five sequential LLM calls" plus a separate totals check. Likewise the gate belongs after step 1 (extraction) and before the downstream LLM steps, not "between the first two steps" when step 2 is itself the validation.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option A to: "A prompt-chaining workflow with one LLM call per extraction/classification/drafting/translation step and a programmatic totals check as the gate after extraction, before the downstream steps." Adjust the explanation's "each fixed step is one call" accordingly.

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is verbatim the first sentence of the explanation, so the entire production-database half of the answer (reserved DB instance, 1- or 3-year commitment, what is and is not discounted) is handed to the learner in the question itself.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint, or replace it with a non-answer nudge such as "Hint: consider commitment-based pricing for steady workloads and what RDS does to an instance that stays stopped."

findings.message: In "For longer gaps take a snapshot and delete it," the pronoun "it" reads as the snapshot rather than the DB instance, which reverses the intended advice.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to "For longer gaps, take a final snapshot and delete the DB instance, then restore from the snapshot when it is needed again."

findings.message: The keyed option says to "recreate the cache as a replication group", but a single-node ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey cluster (cluster mode disabled) is already a replication group with zero replicas — replicas can be added in place and Multi-AZ enabled without recreating anything, so the option teaches an unnecessary and disruptive step.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option (a) to: "Add at least one read replica in a different Availability Zone to the existing replication group, enable Multi-AZ with automatic failover, and point the application at the primary endpoint."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the question at all: the stem asks what changed in a model migration that blanked the reasoning UI and what the thinking display options are (as of 2026-09), but the explanation is entirely about steering Claude toward flowing prose and away from markdown. A learner is given no correct answer and is taught unrelated content as if it were the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with an answer to the stem: describe the thinking/extended-thinking configuration change between the two models (e.g. that the newer model no longer returns raw thinking blocks by default, so a client hard-coded to read them renders nothing) and enumerate the supported display options shown in the code snippet (e.g. summarized vs. raw/none) and how to set them explicitly.

findings.message: The explanation references "Claude Fable 5.1", which is not a real Claude model and does not match either model named in the stem (Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5), so the caution cannot be verified or acted on.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the sentence or replace "Claude Fable 5.1" with the actual model under discussion (Claude Sonnet 5).

findings.message: Option D disqualifies itself in its own text ("without creating permission sets or account assignments"), so no learner needs any knowledge of Identity Center to eliminate it; it tests nothing.
findings.suggestedFix: Make D a plausible but wrong design, e.g. "Enable IAM Identity Center and create permission sets for dev and prod, but keep issuing long-term access keys from the identity account for CLI use."

findings.message: The Anthropic Messages API has no top-level `cache_control` request field: `cache_control` is a property of individual content blocks (in `system`, `messages`, `tools`), so the request body in the code snippet would be rejected as an unexpected parameter rather than enabling "automatic caching" with a self-advancing breakpoint. The described behavior (breakpoint auto-moved to the last cacheable block each turn, consuming one of the 4 breakpoint slots, 400 on TTL conflict) and the Bedrock caveat are not documented API behavior.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the card around the actual mechanism: to cache a growing conversation, set `"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}` on the last content block of the most recent turn (and typically keep a second breakpoint on the stable system/tools prefix), re-marking it each turn; up to 4 breakpoints are allowed and the system checks for hits at prior positions within ~20 blocks. Update the snippet to place cache_control inside a content block, e.g. `"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "...", "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}]`, and drop the top-level field, the invented 400 conditions, and the Bedrock claim unless a source is cited.

findings.message: The answer text is factually wrong when it says "The day 20 step is the fault, not the day 7 step" and "Moving to Standard-IA at day 7 alone is valid." S3 Lifecycle also forbids transitioning objects to S3 Standard-IA or One Zone-IA before they are 30 days old; PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration rejects a STANDARD_IA transition with Days < 30 (InvalidArgument: "'Days' in Transition action must be greater than or equal to 30 for storageClass 'STANDARD_IA'"). So the day 7 step is rejected too, and the rule as written fails validation on both steps.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the answer: S3 rejects both steps. The day 7 transition is invalid because objects must be at least 30 days old before a lifecycle rule can move them to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA, and the day 20 transition is invalid because a Deep Archive transition must be at least 30 days after the Standard-IA transition (e.g., Standard-IA at day 30 and Deep Archive at day 60 or later). Consider also rewording the stem (for example day 30 to Standard-IA and day 45 to Deep Archive) if the intent is to isolate only the second-transition spacing rule.

findings.message: The explanation ends with "The distractor blames the day 7 IA step or accepts the rule unchanged," but this is a question-and-answer card (mcq is null), so there are no options or distractors for the learner to see; the sentence is leftover MCQ authoring text.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the final sentence about the distractor, or convert the card to an MCQ with those options.

findings.message: The explanation's phrase "a peered VPC in another Region" implies that a peered VPC in the same Region could use the gateway endpoint; in fact gateway endpoints cannot be reached through a VPC peering connection at all, regardless of Region (nor via VPN/Direct Connect/transit gateway).
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "...traffic originating in the VPC that contains the endpoint; an on-premises network, any peered VPC, or a transit gateway path needs an interface endpoint instead."

findings.message: The realWorldUsage note claims "a regional NAT gateway expands across zones on its own," but AWS NAT gateways are zonal resources only — there is no regional/multi-AZ NAT gateway, so this teaches a false fact that also contradicts the card's own explanation that a NAT gateway is redundant only inside its own zone.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "NAT gateways are always zonal, so any multi-AZ design needs one gateway per Availability Zone plus a per-subnet route table pointing at the local gateway — the extra gateway alone is not the fix."

findings.message: The explanation's last sentence ("Interface endpoints reach only AWS services, not an external API.") rebuts an option that does not exist on this card — no option mentions VPC interface endpoints — which will confuse learners looking for the matching choice.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the sentence about interface endpoints, or add an interface-endpoint distractor option that it explains.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the question at all: the stem asks which of Lambda or Fargate runs four described workloads and what shortens cold starts, but the explanation describes AWS Lake Formation permissions, Glue Data Catalog, LF-Tags and Athena/Redshift enforcement. A learner would be taught an answer that is factually unrelated and wrong for this stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with content that answers the stem, e.g.: Lambda for the bursty API (fast scale, per-request billing) and the S3-triggered thumbnailer; Fargate for the nightly 40-minute report (exceeds Lambda's 15-minute limit); Lambda with SQS event source mapping and batching for the 200,000 small messages. Cold starts are shortened by provisioned concurrency or SnapStart, smaller deployment packages/fewer dependencies, lazy loading, and initializing SDK clients and DB connections outside the handler so they are reused by warm invocations.

findings.message: The code snippet and realWorldUsage literally state the cold-start part of the answer ("Created once per environment, reused by every warm invocation" / "Create the database connection and SDK clients outside the handler..."), so the learner can read that half of the answer off the card without knowing the topic.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the giveaway comment and move the reuse guidance into the explanation only, e.g. show the snippet without the explanatory comment and drop the realWorldUsage sentence that restates the answer.

findings.message: The stem bundles five separate decisions (four workload placements plus cold-start mitigation) into one card, which cannot be graded as a single recall item even after the explanation is fixed.
findings.suggestedFix: Split into focused cards, e.g. one on why the 40-minute nightly report must run on Fargate rather than Lambda, and one on techniques that shorten Lambda cold starts.

findings.message: Option c's "why" describes the failure mode backwards for an allow-only rule: items like "options before the URL, a different protocol… or a URL in a shell variable" do not match the pattern, so they are not pre-approved and would prompt rather than "slip past" it. The real reasons the control fails are that an allow rule is not a runtime network boundary (a matching command can follow redirects off github.com) and that non-matching commands are still executed in an autonomous/bypass-permissions session, plus other tools and interpreters can make requests.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite c's why as: "Permission patterns only decide whether a command is pre-approved; they do not constrain the network at runtime. A command matching the pattern can still follow a redirect off github.com, and any command that does not match is simply left to the permission prompt — which an autonomous session has nobody to answer, or auto-approves in bypass mode. Other tools and interpreters can also make requests."

findings.message: The stated per-request image cap is wrong: the Claude Messages API documents a maximum of 100 images per API request (20 per turn on claude.ai), not "up to 600 images (100 on models with a 200k-token context window)". Teaching a 600-image ceiling would lead learners to build batches that the API rejects.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "On the Claude API a request may include up to 100 images (claude.ai allows 20 per turn)."

findings.message: The per-image file size figure is inverted/inflated: the Claude API limit is 5 MB per image (with lower platform-specific caps on Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex AI), not 10 MB on the Claude API with 5 MB on Bedrock/Vertex.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "each image at most 5 MB and 8000 by 8000 px; Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex AI impose their own, lower per-image size limits."

findings.message: The explanation dismisses a distractor that does not exist on this card: it says "self-managed Kafka on EC2 keeps the operational burden of sizing and patching brokers," but there is no EC2/self-managed Kafka option among a-d. This will confuse a learner comparing the rationale to the options.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the clause about self-managed Kafka on EC2 (or add a fifth option "Run self-managed Apache Kafka on Amazon EC2" with a matching "why").

findings.message: Option b is the only option that mentions the sensor/time-series half of the scenario at all (c and f address only the relationship traversal; d and e say "both features"), and it echoes the stem's distinctive phrase "sensor readings". A learner who knows nothing about AWS databases can pick b from that wording alone, so half the keyed pair is given away without any topic knowledge.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a genuine distractor for the time-series half that also names the sensor data, e.g. "Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a timestamp-indexed readings table and scheduled deletes for the sensor readings", so option b is no longer the only option addressing that feature.

findings.message: Option d repeats option a's text verbatim (Firehose buffering into tens-of-MB objects) and only adds an irrelevant runbook sentence, so it is just as correct as the keyed option a; a learner cannot choose a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d's text with the distractor the explanation and its "why" clearly intend, e.g. "Keep one PutObject per reading but enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket."

findings.message: Option d's "why" discusses S3 Transfer Acceleration, which appears nowhere in option d's text, so it fails to explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the "why" with the option text (once option d is rewritten as the Transfer Acceleration distractor, the existing "why" becomes accurate).

findings.message: The explanation lists "fable" as a valid value for the subagent `model` frontmatter field. There is no such Claude model alias; the accepted aliases are sonnet, opus, haiku, inherit (plus opusplan) or a full model id, so learners would memorize a non-existent value.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "model can be sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full model id or inherit" to "model can be sonnet, opus, haiku, a full model id, or inherit (to use the parent's model)".

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is copied verbatim from the first sentence of the explanation, so it gives away the answer to the first two parts of the question (where the definition lives and that name/description are required) without any knowledge of the topic.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Hint line from the question, or replace it with a non-answering nudge such as "Hint: think about what context a freshly spawned agent does and does not inherit."

findings.message: Option d's rationale says "after 25 bloated results have already cost money and attention," but the stem states a typical session runs 30 searches (and the 100k-token threshold in that option corresponds to 25 hits at 4k tokens each only coincidentally). The mismatched number is a factual inconsistency within the card.
findings.suggestedFix: Change option d's "why" to reference the stem's numbers, e.g. "...it treats the symptom only after roughly 25 of the session's 30 bloated results (100k tokens) have already cost money and attention..."

findings.message: Option C invents a command and a setting that do not exist: Claude Code has no `/autocompact` slash command and no adjustable "auto-compact window" (auto-compact is a toggle, historically under `/config`). Teaching the option with a fabricated command weakens the card even though the option is correctly keyed as wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option C to use a real mechanism, e.g. "Leave CLAUDE.md as is and rely on auto-compaction to shrink the conversation once the window fills.", and adjust its "why" to note that compaction only trims conversation history while CLAUDE.md is re-injected at every session start.

findings.message: The explanation says a VPC link private integration "reaches an internal NLB or ALB," but for REST APIs a VPC link only targets an internal Network Load Balancer; ALB (and Cloud Map) targets are supported only by HTTP API VPC links. Since the stem explicitly requires a REST API fronting a service behind an internal ALB, the card teaches an unworkable mapping (the real pattern is an internal NLB in front of the ALB, or an HTTP API).
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "A REST API VPC link private integration targets an internal Network Load Balancer only; to reach a service behind an internal ALB from a REST API, place an internal NLB in front of the ALB (HTTP API VPC links can target an ALB directly)."

findings.message: "The integration timeout defaults to 29 seconds (50 ms minimum); it is a hard limit that no API type can raise" is no longer true. Since June 2024 the 29-second integration timeout is an adjustable quota for Regional and private REST APIs (and HTTP APIs), so it can be raised via a service quota increase; only edge-optimized REST APIs keep the hard 29-second cap.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with: "The integration timeout defaults to 29 seconds (50 ms minimum). For Regional and private REST APIs (and HTTP APIs) this is an adjustable quota that can be raised via a service quota increase, though edge-optimized REST APIs remain capped at 29 seconds; even so, a two-minute job is better handled by returning 202 and completing asynchronously via SQS or Step Functions."

findings.message: The explanation refutes a "Snowball" option ("Snowball is offline bulk transfer with no change capture") that does not exist among the four options, which will confuse learners comparing the explanation to the choices.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Snowball sentence from the explanation, or add a fifth option using AWS Snowball for offline bulk transfer so the rebuttal matches an actual choice.

findings.message: The stem's premise is inconsistent with the documented API limit: images sent inline must be no larger than 5 MB each (and base64 encoding adds ~33% overhead), so a 6 MB photo could not be embedded as base64 on turn one at all.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the size to a value under the inline limit, e.g. "receives a 4 MB photo on turn one", or state that the photo is resized to fit the 5 MB inline limit before being base64-encoded.

findings.message: Option D's rationale asserts that "SSE-C has been blocked by default on new buckets since April 2026" — no such AWS change exists; SSE-C remains fully supported on S3 buckets (it can only be restricted by customer-authored bucket policies or an SCP). The card teaches a fabricated fact as a reason to reject the option.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the clause "and SSE-C has been blocked by default on new buckets since April 2026"; the remaining reasons (no key policy to revoke, no KMS Decrypt audit entry, client must transmit keys) are sufficient and accurate.

findings.message: The explanation's claim that S3 Bucket Keys "stop checking the key policy" is false: KMS permissions (including the key policy) are still evaluated on every KMS call S3 makes for the bucket-level key; Bucket Keys only reduce how often those calls occur and change the encryption context to the bucket ARN, which is what weakens per-object auditing.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "...but they log the bucket ARN instead of the object ARN and reuse a bucket-level key so most requests make no KMS call at all, so leave them off when the audit must be per object."

findings.message: Option e (character counts divided by four) is a crude rule-of-thumb estimate that no learner searching for the MOST accurate, invoice-reconcilable source would plausibly select, so it adds no discrimination to the item.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option e with a plausible-but-wrong source, e.g. "The Console Usage dashboard's aggregated daily charts exported as CSV" and explain in 'why' that the dashboard aggregates without per-request cache-hit detail needed for the cache metric.

findings.message: Option a states both endpoints can be "grouped by workspace and model", but the Admin API cost_report supports grouping only by workspace_id and description (model appears inside description); only usage_report supports group_by=model.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option a to: "The Usage and Cost Admin API (usage_report grouped by workspace and model, cost_report grouped by workspace and description), called with an Admin API key."

findings.message: The claim that "role sessions (EC2, Lambda, AssumeRole) carry no MFA information, so the key reads false" is wrong for AssumeRole calls that pass MFA (SerialNumber/TokenCode): those role sessions do carry MFA context, so aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true for requests made with them. The statement is only true for sessions obtained without MFA, such as EC2 instance-profile, Lambda execution-role, and plain AssumeRole sessions.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "The trap: role sessions created without MFA (EC2 instance profiles, Lambda execution roles, plain AssumeRole) carry no MFA context, so the key reads false and an MFA Deny in an SCP blocks every workload role. Only sessions from an AssumeRole call that supplied SerialNumber/TokenCode (or GetSessionToken with MFA) report the key as true — so enforce MFA in the human roles' trust policies on sts:AssumeRole instead."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the question at all: the stem asks which AWS service runs mobile/browser tests on real hardware (AWS Device Farm) and what it is not built for, but the explanation is entirely about Amazon SQS long polling, ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds, visibility timeout and delay queues. A learner would be given a wrong, unrelated answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with Device Farm content, e.g.: "AWS Device Farm runs your app and Selenium/Appium test suites on real, physical Android and iOS devices and on real desktop browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) in the AWS Cloud, returning videos, logs and performance data per device. It is functional/compatibility testing on real hardware — it is not a load- or performance-testing service for your backend (use Distributed Load Testing on AWS or a load-testing tool for that), and it does not test server-side APIs."

findings.message: The second half of the stem, "what is it not built for", has no deciding criterion, so many different answers are defensible (not for backend load testing, not for unit testing, not for emulator-only testing, not for production monitoring). The learner cannot know which negative case is intended.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the contrast explicit, e.g.: "Which AWS service runs these tests on real devices and desktop browsers, and why is it not the right choice for generating high-volume load against your backend?"

findings.message: The support-plan requirement for the AWS Health API is stated incorrectly: access requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan. There is no AWS Support plan called "Unified Operations," and listing "Enterprise" separately after "Business Support+" is redundant.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "needs a Business Support+, Enterprise or Unified Operations plan" with "requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan".

findings.message: The keyed answer is option d ("Compare published benchmark scores and pick the higher one"), which is factually wrong and is even refuted by its own "why" text and by the card's explanation; the correct basis described in the explanation is option a (dollars per successfully fixed build on a tail-weighted sample), which is marked correct: false.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option a and "correct": false on option d, give option a a null/affirming rationale, and keep d's existing "why" as the distractor explanation.

findings.message: Option c's rationale states that SNS "retries a failed delivery only three times by default and never for more than an hour"; the default SNS delivery policy for HTTP/S endpoints is 50 attempts (3 immediate, 2 at 1s, 10 with exponential backoff, 35 at 20s) spread over roughly 20+ minutes, so the card teaches an incorrect retry fact.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "SNS pushes each notification as it arrives and, once its delivery retries are exhausted, the message is discarded unless a DLQ is attached; with no queue in front of the workers there is nothing to absorb the spike and nothing to hand a crashed worker's image to another one."

findings.message: The explanation dismisses "Kinesis Data Streams" as an incorrect choice, but no option mentions Kinesis, which will confuse learners comparing the explanation to the four options.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Kinesis clause from the explanation (or add a Kinesis Data Streams distractor option so the rebuttal matches).

findings.message: The keyed option's value "claude-3-opus-20240229" is a legacy Claude 3 Opus identifier that is inconsistent with the card's own "claude-sonnet-5" era and is a deprecated model, so a learner copying it may configure a model that no longer resolves.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a current Opus alias in the keyed option, e.g. Add "model": "opus" (or the current claude-opus-* ID) to .claude/settings.local.json.

findings.message: Option (a) is self-defeating on its face ("ask teammates to ignore the diff"), so no learner would seriously consider it; it does not test knowledge of settings precedence.
findings.suggestedFix: Make (a) a plausible shared-file action, e.g. "Add \"model\": \"opus\" to the committed .claude/settings.json under a per-user comment", with a why explaining that shared project settings apply to everyone who clones the repo.

findings.message: Option D contains exactly the same configuration as the keyed option A (Read(**/.env) and Read(**/.env.*) deny rules in shared .claude/settings.json) plus a documentation step, so it satisfies the requirement and the 'MOST reliable' qualifier at least as well as A; a learner cannot choose between them.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option D with a genuinely weaker alternative that matches its rationale, e.g. 'Add Edit(**/.env) and Edit(**/.env.*) deny rules to permissions.deny and rely on them for both reading and writing.'

findings.message: Option D's 'why' talks about Edit-only deny rules leaving Read/Grep/cat open, which does not describe option D's text (Read deny rules plus a runbook entry), so it fails to explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite option D's 'why' so it matches the option's actual text (or, if the option is changed to an Edit-only rule as suggested, the existing 'why' becomes accurate).

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST highly available", but the keyed option is not the best on availability: S3 Standard-IA (which the lifecycle rule moves 80%+ of the data into after 60 days) is designed for 99.9% availability, while an EFS Regional file system (option B) is designed for 99.99%, the same as S3 Standard. All of the explanation and the option rationales argue cost ($/GB-month, retrieval fees), never availability or SLAs, so the keyed answer is justified against a qualifier the stem does not state.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the stem and the mcq qualifier to the cost criterion the card actually tests: "Which storage service is the MOST cost-effective home for this library?" with qualifier "MOST cost-effective" (matching the topic "4.1 Cost-optimized storage"). If availability is really the intended axis, rewrite the explanation and option rationales around S3's 99.99% designed availability / 99.9% SLA and drop or justify the Standard-IA lifecycle step.

findings.message: The "why" texts for options B and D explain only that those choices cost more (EFS $0.30/GB-month; Glacier IR retrieval fees), which does not explain why they fail the stem's stated criterion of being the MOST highly available option.
findings.suggestedFix: If the availability qualifier is kept, rewrite B's why to note EFS's serving path and 99.99% availability versus S3's, and D's why to note Glacier Instant Retrieval's 99.9% designed availability plus retrieval characteristics; if the qualifier becomes cost, the existing whys are fine.

findings.message: The code snippet sets output_config.effort on "claude-3-opus-20240229", a Claude 3 model that has no effort support at all (and is retired as of the review date); this directly contradicts the explanation's own support matrix, which limits effort to the 4.6/4.7/4.8/5-generation models, so the snippet models an invalid API call.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the snippet's model to a model the explanation lists as supporting effort, e.g. "model": "claude-opus-5" (or another listed model), keeping the rest of the body unchanged.

findings.message: The stem asks for "the two consequences of changing effort mid-session," but the explanation names only one (a top-level change restarts the prompt cache); the remaining sentences describe effort's general behavior and a beta workaround, not a second consequence of changing it mid-session, so the answer does not cover what the question asks.
findings.suggestedFix: Either state both consequences explicitly (e.g. "(1) the prompt cache is invalidated and re-primed, and (2) output length/tool-call verbosity shifts for all subsequent tokens in the conversation") or reword the stem to "what happens to the prompt cache when you change effort mid-session?"

findings.message: Option c is explicitly excluded by the stem's constraint "without changing the model," so no learner reading the stem would select it, and its "why" never mentions that it violates the stated constraint.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with a plausible in-scope distractor (e.g., "Add a per-ticket cost budget check that logs a warning when exceeded"), or amend its "why" to state that the stem forbids changing the model.

findings.message: The explanation asserts flatly that "Snowball Edge Storage Optimized holds 210 TB usable, so three devices carry the archive," but Storage Optimized ships in two capacities — the 80 TB HDD model and the 210 TB NVMe model — so the device count is 3 only for the 210TB variant (the 80 TB model would need 7). The unqualified figure could mislead a learner who is tested on the 80 TB number.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "The Snowball Edge Storage Optimized 210TB device holds 210 TB usable, so three devices carry the archive (the older 80 TB Storage Optimized model would need seven)."

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST cost-effective", but the card actually tests secure tenant isolation, and cost is never the deciding factor; by the stated cost criterion option B (add a sentence to the system prompt, changing nothing else) is by far the cheapest to build and run, so the keyed answer does not best satisfy the qualifier.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the stem's qualifier to a security criterion, e.g. "Which design change is REQUIRED to prevent one customer from reading another customer's file?" and set mcq.qualifier accordingly (e.g. "required for tenant isolation").

findings.message: The keyed option prescribes "a workspace per tenant" for a SaaS with "many customers", but Console workspaces are an administrative construct with per-organization limits and are not intended to scale to arbitrary end-customer counts; the essential fix is server-side file-ID mapping and authorization, with per-workspace separation only where tenant counts allow.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword the key to emphasize the authorization layer, e.g. "Keep file IDs server-side and authorize each request against your own user-to-file mapping, using separate workspaces/scoped keys where the tenant count permits.", and soften the same claim in the explanation.

findings.message: Option (a) keys "three" Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices as sufficient for 500 TB, which only works for the 210 TB NVMe variant; the long-documented Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device holds ~80 TB usable, and a learner using that figure would compute seven devices, making the keyed count look wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Name the capacity in the option, e.g. "Order three Snowball Edge Storage Optimized 210 TB devices (630 TB usable), copy the 500 TB onto them and ship them back for import into S3."

findings.message: Option e (client began logging the request-id response header) is implausible as a cache-invalidation cause — a client-side logging change to a response header obviously cannot alter the request prefix, so no learner would select it.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a plausible near-miss, e.g. "A second cache_control breakpoint was added after the last user message" or "The tools array was reordered without changing any tool text", with a "why" explaining precisely why it does or does not invalidate the prefix.

findings.message: Option e self-identifies as running "at the origin" while the stem explicitly asks for "edge placements", so no learner would select it; its "why" also omits the stronger objection that ALB listener rules cannot rewrite URLs or add request headers at all (they support only forward, redirect, fixed-response and authenticate actions).
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option e with a plausible edge option, e.g. "Run a Lambda@Edge function on the viewer response event to add the security header and call DynamoDB", and set its "why" to explain that viewer response runs after the origin has been contacted and on every request, so it cannot enrich the request before the origin sees it.

findings.message: The "LOWEST cost" qualifier does no discriminating work: SCPs, per-account IAM policies and disabling Regions are all free, so options A, B and D tie on cost and only C (AWS Config) has a charge. The real deciding criterion is preventive, centrally enforced control that account administrators cannot remove, which the stem states but the qualifier does not reflect.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier to something the key uniquely satisfies, e.g. "Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?" (and update the stem wording accordingly), or drop the cost qualifier and ask simply "Which solution meets these requirements?"

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key.", which is verbatim the first sentence of the explanation/answer. A learner with no knowledge of S3 encryption can recite the answer straight from the question.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint line from the question, or replace it with a non-revealing cue such as "Hint: consider which option logs key usage in CloudTrail and lets you scope a key policy per dataset."

findings.message: The realWorldUsage claim that S3 server access log destination buckets must stay on SSE-S3 is no longer accurate: since 2023 S3 supports delivering server access logs to buckets using SSE-KMS when an S3 Bucket Key is enabled. Also, the stated failure mode is wrong — without Bucket Keys log delivery simply fails rather than producing objects encrypted with an unreadable key.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "Destination buckets for S3 server access logs can use SSE-S3, or SSE-KMS provided an S3 Bucket Key is enabled on the bucket; with plain SSE-KMS and no Bucket Key, log delivery fails."

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST cost-effective", but cost is not what separates the options — the deciding criterion is security effectiveness. Option B (leave the tool unrestricted, rely on the built-in prior-context rule) requires zero configuration and no added spend, and option D explicitly lowers token cost, so both satisfy "cost-effective" at least as well as the keyed allowlist answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier to a security criterion, e.g. "Which configuration MOST effectively limits exfiltration risk while keeping the feature?" (and set mcq.qualifier to "MOST effectively limits exfiltration risk").

findings.message: The keyed option is the only one that repeats the distinctive host name "docs.example.com" from the stem; a learner who knows nothing about web_fetch configuration can match that string and pick A without reasoning about allowlists versus denylists or token limits.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the literal host from the key (e.g. "Set allowed_domains to only your knowledge-base host and a small max_uses on the web_fetch tool definition") or make the other options reference the same host, e.g. "Add a blocked_domains list of known malicious hosts while leaving docs.example.com and all other domains reachable."

findings.message: The keyed option is the only one that carries its own justification ("because on Foundry the model parameter is the deployment name, which only defaults to the model ID"), making it noticeably longer and more explanatory than the three distractors, which weakens discrimination even though it is not a direct wording leak.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim option b to a parallel, assertion-only form such as "Send the deployment name the admin chose in the Foundry portal instead of the model ID." and move the rationale into the explanation field, where it already appears.

findings.message: Option D is implausible on two counts: cross-zone load balancing is already enabled by default on an Application Load Balancer and cannot be turned off at the load balancer level (only per target group), so "enable" it is a no-op, and inbound request distribution is plainly unrelated to NatGateway-Bytes or idle Elastic IP charges. The "why" does not mention that it is already on by default.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option D with a more tempting cost lever, e.g. "Create interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon S3 in each private subnet", and explain in its "why" that interface endpoints add $0.01/hour per AZ plus per-GB charges while a gateway endpoint is free; or keep D but note in the "why" that ALB cross-zone load balancing is on by default and free, so enabling it changes nothing.

findings.message: The stated batch size limits are wrong: the Anthropic Message Batches API allows up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch (whichever comes first), not 10,000 requests or 32 MB. The explanation is also internally inconsistent, since 150,000 requests would need 15 batches under a 10,000-request cap, not two, and the realWorldUsage note correctly says to split into 100,000-request batches.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "A Message Batch holds at most 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first, so 150,000 needs two batches."

findings.message: Fargate's maximum task size is 16 vCPU with 120 GB of memory, not 32 vCPU with 244 GB; the largest documented CPU value is 16384 CPU units paired with 32–120 GB memory.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "up to 32 vCPU with 244 GB" to "up to 16 vCPU with 120 GB".

findings.message: Fargate tasks get 20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default, and since platform version 1.4.0 the ephemeralStorage parameter lets you request up to 200 GiB, so "10 GiB ... with no option to request more" is false and would mislead learners about a key Fargate limit.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default, configurable up to 200 GiB via the ephemeralStorage task definition parameter (platform version 1.4.0 or later)".

findings.message: Option b is verbatim the keyed option a plus an irrelevant extra step ("Record the change in the team's runbook"), so it is equally correct and a learner cannot pick a single answer; option b's "why" also argues against a CLAUDE.md option that does not exist in the list (the explanation likewise cites CLAUDE.md as a distractor).
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option b's text with the intended CLAUDE.md distractor, e.g. "Append the full procedure to .claude/CLAUDE.md so it is always available.", which matches its existing "why" and the explanation.

findings.message: The explanation ends with "the distractor is an interface endpoint for S3", but this is a question-and-answer card (mcq is null) with no options, so there is no distractor for the learner to see.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the closing clause with a direct statement, e.g. "Do not use an interface endpoint for S3 here: it is billed per AZ-hour and per GB, while the gateway endpoint is free."

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: the correct option begins \"An AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint backed by the S3 ...\"", which quotes the keyed option's opening words verbatim; a learner with no AWS knowledge can pick option A from that cue alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint line so the stem ends at "Which design meets this with the LEAST operational overhead?"

findings.message: Option d restates option b verbatim ("send one request built by the same code through the synchronous Messages API and fail the job if it returns a 400") and only adds a runbook note, so it is just as correct as the keyed option b; a learner cannot pick a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d with a genuinely different, incorrect safeguard, e.g. "Filter out any requests whose results come back errored and report only the successful documents." (which matches the existing 'why' about discarding errors).

findings.message: Option d's "why" ("Discarding errors hides the 30% of documents that were never processed...") does not describe option d's text at all, which says nothing about discarding errors.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite option d's "why" so it explains why that specific option is wrong, or change option d's text to the error-discarding approach the "why" already describes.

findings.message: The card keys option B (cross-Region read replica / pilot light) as correct, but that option's own "why" text explains why it is wrong, and the explanation, qualifier ("MOST cost-effective") and realWorldUsage all identify the AWS Backup cross-Region copy plus CloudFormation approach (option A) as the answer. Option B keeps a replica billed continuously to beat a 24-hour RPO/RTO the business never required, so it is not the most cost-effective choice.
findings.suggestedFix: Set option A "correct": true and option B "correct": false, and give option A "why": null while keeping B's existing explanation as its distractor rationale.

findings.message: Option c is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option a (only prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), yet it is keyed incorrect. Two identical answers — one correct, one wrong — make it impossible for a learner to select a single intended answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with the distinct distractor its "why" was written for, e.g. "Create replacement keys and re-encrypt every ciphertext (and re-sign every artifact) under the new keys so the old keys can be retired."

findings.message: Option c's "why" (about KMS retaining old material so mass re-encryption is never required) does not explain anything wrong with option c's actual text, which contains no re-encryption step.
findings.suggestedFix: After replacing option c's text with a re-encryption distractor, keep the existing rationale; otherwise rewrite the "why" to match the option text.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks about the isolation boundary for Files API uploads, but the answer text describes tool_choice.disable_parallel_tool_use and parallel tool use semantics. As written the card teaches a learner nothing correct about file scoping, and the realWorldUsage note (per-tenant workspaces) contradicts it.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the correct answer, e.g.: "Files uploaded via the Files API are scoped to the workspace that owns the API key, not to the individual key. Every API key in the Default Workspace can list, download and delete every other tenant's files, so one-key-per-customer provides no isolation. Create a separate workspace per tenant (or per isolation boundary) and issue that tenant's keys from it; files then cannot be accessed across workspaces."

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: the correct option begins \"Upload each screenshot once to the Files API and reference ...\"", which literally quotes the opening of keyed option A. Any learner, regardless of knowledge, can pick the key by string matching, and shuffling the options does not help.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint line so the stem ends at "...without losing earlier screenshots?"

findings.message: The explanation ends with "A bucket cannot hold an ACM certificate; S3 already terminates TLS with its own," but no option mentions ACM or certificates, so this rebuts a distractor that does not exist on the card.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the ACM sentence, or replace it with a note tied to an actual option (e.g., restate why the SSE-KMS or Block Public Access options fail the in-transit requirement).

findings.message: "the condition is true only for HTTPS requests, so plain HTTP is rejected" is backwards as written: the deny condition (aws:SecureTransport = false) evaluates true only for plain HTTP requests, which is why they are denied. As phrased it implies the deny fires on HTTPS.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "aws:SecureTransport is true only for HTTPS requests, so the Deny matches exactly the plain-HTTP requests and S3 rejects them itself, with nothing to run or maintain."

findings.message: Advising to "add a NumericLessThan condition on s3:TlsVersion 1.2" to the same Deny statement is technically wrong: conditions within one statement are ANDed, and plain-HTTP requests carry no s3:TlsVersion value, so the combined statement would stop denying HTTP altogether.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "To also insist on a modern protocol, add a second Deny statement with NumericLessThan on s3:TlsVersion 1.2 (a separate statement, since conditions inside one statement are ANDed)."

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST highly available", but nothing in the card evaluates availability: the keyed answer and every distractor "why" argue purely on cost, and DataSync over a single internet link is not more highly available than a Direct Connect path (a dedicated circuit plus internet failover would arguably be more available). As written the keyed option does not best satisfy the stated qualifier.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the stem and mcq.qualifier to the cost criterion the card actually reasons about, e.g. question: "...Which solution transfers the nightly data at the LOWEST cost?" and qualifier: "LOWEST cost".

findings.message: Option C (send text tickets to Amazon Transcribe and infer mood from transcript confidence scores) is implausible on two counts a learner sees immediately — the input is free text, not audio, and confidence scores are obviously not sentiment — so it is unlikely to attract any candidate.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C with a plausible near-miss, e.g. "Use Amazon Comprehend custom classification: label a sample of tickets, train a custom classifier, and call the custom endpoint for each ticket" (wrong because it requires labelling and a provisioned endpoint, adding cost the pre-trained DetectSentiment API avoids).

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the question at all: the stem asks about federation paths (Okta SSO across dozens of accounts, a standalone account, mobile-app end users uploading to S3) and where IAM users still belong, but the explanation describes AWS Lambda invocation retry behaviour, DLQs, destinations and stream/SQS event sources. A learner would be given an answer that is entirely off-topic and cannot learn the keyed content.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the federation answer, e.g.: "Dozens of accounts with corporate Okta → AWS IAM Identity Center with Okta as the external SAML/SCIM identity provider, using permission sets assigned per account. One standalone account → a direct IAM SAML or OIDC identity provider in that account with IAM roles assumed via AssumeRoleWithSAML/AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Mobile app customers uploading to S3 → Amazon Cognito user pools for sign-in plus identity pools to vend short-lived credentials for a scoped S3 prefix (or have the backend issue pre-signed URLs). IAM users are now only for the few cases with no federation option — for example service or emergency break-glass access and legacy tools that need long-lived access keys — and should have MFA and rotated keys."

findings.message: The explanation says batch is "not a faster or cheaper version of the same call," which contradicts the card's own (correct) statement that the Batches API carries a 50% discount; batch is literally cheaper, it is just not lower-latency.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "...batch is a pricing tier bought with latency: 50% cheaper for the same call, but asynchronous and best-effort within 24 hours, so it cannot serve a two-second path."

findings.message: Option D's rationale lists "fast mode and data residency" as documented per-token price modifiers for the Anthropic API; the published modifiers are prompt caching, batch processing and long-context/model tiering, so these invented modifiers could mislead learners even though the option's core point (time of day does not affect price) is right.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the why to: "Standard API prices are per token by model, with documented modifiers such as prompt caching and batch processing; time of day is not one of them, so rescheduling changes nothing on the bill and leaves the genuinely batchable workload on the full-price API."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the question at all: the stem asks about S3 cross-Region replication (versioning requirements on both buckets, why CRR does not cover pre-existing objects, and where CRR sits among replication mechanisms), but the explanation describes Application Migration Service, Application Discovery Service, Migration Hub and DMS. A learner would be taught nothing correct about the asked topic, and would be left with an answer that is false for this stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with S3 replication content, e.g.: "Both the source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled, and the source bucket needs an IAM role that S3 can assume to read objects and write to the destination. Enabling a CRR rule only replicates objects created or updated after the rule is in place, so last year's objects are not copied; to backfill existing objects you must run S3 Batch Replication (an S3 Batch Operations job) on the existing objects. Among S3 replication mechanisms, CRR is the cross-Region form of S3 Replication (SRR replicates within one Region, Multi-Region Access Points plus two-way replication rules give active-active), and it is asynchronous, so use it for compliance/DR copies rather than for synchronous consistency. Also check the object ReplicationStatus (PENDING/COMPLETED/FAILED) to verify."
